11. Issue no.4:
Whether the present suit has not been signed, verified and filed by a competent person, as alleged?
The burden of proving this issue was fixed upon the defendant.

11.2. As per Order VI Rule 14 and 15 CPC, the plaint can be signed and verified either by the plaintiff,
or by the person duly authorized by him to do so.
Further, as per Order III Rule 1 CPC, an appearance, an application or an Act can be made or done either by the party in person, or by his recognized agent.

As per Rule 2, a person holding Power of Attorney, therein authorized to appear before the Court, or to make an application, or to do any other act on behalf of the party to the suit,
is a recognized agent.

12.2. The case of the defendant no.2 was that she was not involved in the discussion for investment,
or in the transactions with the plaintiff, or in the construction/development of the suit property.
She has also claimed that she was neither a party to any document/agreement with respect to the suit property executed with the plaintiff, nor did she receive any money from the plaintiff.
She has claimed that she is, thus, neither a necessary party, nor a proper party.
She has further claimed that she has been unnecessarily impleaded in the suit for the purpose of harassing her and extorting money from her.

12.3. As per Order I Rule 3 CPC, more than one person can be joined as defendants where any right to relief in respect of same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist against such persons, whether jointly, severally, or in the alternative; and where if separate suits were brought against such persons, any common question of law or fact would arise.

Thus, it is necessary that a right to relief in favour of the plaintiff should be alleged to be v.
Jagdish Balwani & Anr.
Digitally signed SACHIN by SACHIN MITTAL MITTAL Date: 2025.05.15 13:08:04 +0530 existing against the act or transaction of the defendants impleaded in the suit.
It is not necessary that the plaintiff should claim relief against each and every person impleaded as defendant in the suit.

The general rule is that the plaintiff, being the dominus litis/master of his suit,
has right to decide as to against whom he needs relief and whom to implead as defendant in his suit.
A person may be joined in a suit either as a necessary party, or as a proper party.

There are two tests for determining the question whether a particular party is a necessary party to a proceeding: (i)
there must be a right to some relief against such party in respect of the matter involved in the proceeding in question; and (ii) it should not be possible to pass an effective decree in absence of such a party.

A proper party, on the other hand, is a person whose presence would enable the court to completely, effectively and properly adjudicate upon all matters and issues, though he may not be a person in favour of or against whom a decree is to be made.

12.4. Here, it would be relevant to note that the defendant no.2 was not a party to the collaboration agreement dated 13.03.2013, or to the agreement to sell dated 17.03.2013, or to the confirmation agreement dated 17.03.2013, or to the cancellation deed dated 01.09.2014.
Further, the plaintiff has also failed to prove that he had paid any amount towards sale consideration to the defendant no.2.

Even, the two cheques admittedly were issued by the defendant no.1.
12.5.
The plaintiff has filed the present suit for the recovery of unpaid advance sale consideration paid to the defendant no.1.

The said sale consideration admittedly having been paid to the defendant no.1 only pursuant to agreement to sell dated 17.03.2013 with him, the same cannot be sought to be recovered from the defendant no.2.
Having said this, the plaintiff has attributed in the plaint role of the defendant no.2 in the transaction with him.

The allegations/ averments against defendant no. 2 in the plaint were sufficient for her impleadment in the present suit.

12.6. In view of the above discussion, though the present suit cannot be said to be bad for misjoinder of parties, it is held that the defendant no.2 for want of privity of contract is not liable for the relief(s) sought by the plaintiff.
The issue no.3 is determined accordingly.

OPP Issue no.2: Whether plaintiff is entitled to 12% interest pendente lite and future on the aforesaid amount against the defendants, as prayed for?
The burden of proving both these issues was upon the plaintiff.
13.2. The case of the plaintiff is that the defendants, out of total payment of Rs.1 crore, have only refunded a sum of Rs.8 lakhs, and a sum of Rs.92 lakhs is still due and payable from them.
The plaintiff claims that the defendants are liable to pay the said amount of Rs.92 lakhs alongwith a sum of Rs.40,07,671/- towards interest at the rate of 12% per annum for the pre-suit period.
The plaintiff is also seeking the recovery of the pendente lite and future interest at the rate of 12% per annum.

Further, the plaintiff through the bank witness, PW-3 has also proved dishonour of two cheques issued by the defendant no.1 towards part refund of the sale consideration of Rs.1 crore paid by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff through the bank witness, PW-7 has also proved statement of his bank account for the purpose of proving the payment made to the defendant no.1 through various cheques.
The defendant no.1 has not appeared before this Court for the purpose of controverting the claim of the plaintiff.
There is nothing on record to doubt the veracity of plaintiff's claim for the refund of sale consideration allegedly paid to the defendant no.1.
The plaintiff has also claimed that out of Rs.1 crore he has received a sum of Rs.8 lakhs from the defendant no.1 and a sum of Rs.92 lakhs still remains to be paid by him.
13.4. In view of the above, the defendant no.1 is held liable for the payment of Rs.92 lakhs to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff has also sought recovery of a sum of Rs.40,07,671/- towards pre-suit interest at the rate of 12% per annum.
It is a settled law that the pre-suit interest is to be governed by the terms of contract between the parties.
In the absence of any term regarding pre-suit interest, the same cannot be awarded to the plaintiff.
In the present case, the plaintiff has failed to prove any such term regarding interest in the contract with the defendant no. 1.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
As per Section 20 of the CPC, it is at the time of commencement of the suit, that the defendant(s) should actually be residing or should be carrying on business or should be working for gain within the territorial limits of the Court, before which the suit is instituted.
Such place(s) of the defendant(s), at the time of transaction in question, is irrelevant.
Thus, it is necessary that a right to relief in favour of the plaintiff should be alleged to be v.
Jagdish Balwani & Anr.
It is not necessary that the plaintiff should claim relief against each and every person impleaded as defendant in the suit.
The general rule is that the plaintiff, being the dominus litis/master of his suit,
has right to decide as to against whom he needs relief and whom to implead as defendant in his suit.
A person may be joined in a suit either as a necessary party, or as a proper party.
There are two tests for determining the question whether a particular party is a necessary party to a proceeding: (i)
there must be a right to some relief against such party in respect of the matter involved in the proceeding in question; and (ii) it should not be possible to pass an effective decree in absence of such a party.
A proper party, on the other hand, is a person whose presence would enable the court to completely, effectively and properly adjudicate upon all matters and issues, though he may not be a person in favour of or against whom a decree is to be made.
Further, the plaintiff has also failed to prove that he had paid any amount towards sale consideration to the defendant no.2.
Even, the two cheques admittedly were issued by the defendant no.1.
12.5.
The plaintiff has filed the present suit for the recovery of unpaid advance sale consideration paid to the defendant no.1.
The said sale consideration admittedly having been paid to the defendant no.1 only pursuant to agreement to sell dated 17.03.2013 with him, the same cannot be sought to be recovered from the defendant no.2.
Having said this, the plaintiff has attributed in the plaint role of the defendant no.2 in the transaction with him.
However, merely because the plaintiff has not been able to prove his right to relief against the defendant no.2, the suit cannot be said to be bad for misjoinder of parties.
It is a settled law that the pre-suit interest is to be governed by the terms of contract between the parties.
In the absence of any term regarding pre-suit interest, the same cannot be awarded to the plaintiff.
In the present case, the plaintiff has failed to prove any such term regarding interest in the contract with the defendant no. 1.
